evidence.title: Philippine central bank hastens interest rate rise, ready for more action

evidence.title: Philippines Economic Updates

The source is a government newswire.

evidence.title: Marcos relays food production agenda in 1st SONA

evidence.title: Senate approves 2023 national budget on third reading

evidence.title: Marcos admin streamlines private sector participation processes to encourage investments

evidence.title: DOF unveils fiscal priority reforms under Marcos admin

evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct at the administration level.
contrary_evidence: Proposed reform only; not proof of enactment or anti-corruption impact.
The source is a ministry announcement.

evidence.title: PHILIPPINES: Reducing Inequality Key to Becoming a Middle-Class Society Free of Poverty

The data are not a direct measure of Marcos-specific 2022 outcomes.

It is an aggregate planning metric, not a ruler-specific causal estimate.

evidence.title: Marcos' 1st edict abolishes PACC, Office of CabSec

evidence.title: Gov't told not to abolish PCGG during Marcos rule

evidence.title: PinasLakas vaccination launch

evidence.title: DOH achieves major strides in fight vs COVID-19, strengthens PH healthcare system

evidence.title: DepEd develops learning recovery plan as more schools conduct face-to-face classes

chapter_notes.RECON:
Using your local prior as the structured baseline, and not touching the client matrix, here is the compact research frame for Bongbong Marcos in 2022.

**Office, Authority, Constraints**
- Marcos was proclaimed president-elect on **May 25, 2022** and sworn in on **June 30, 2022**. That makes **June 30, 2022** the start of the ruler period for 2022.
- His office is the Philippine presidency. Under **Article VII of the 1987 Constitution**, executive power is vested in the President, the term begins at **noon on June 30**, and the President has control over executive departments and offices.
- A concrete example of that authority is **Executive Order No. 1** on **June 30, 2022**, which reorganized the Office of the President and abolished the Presidential Anti-Corruption Commission and the Office of the Cabinet Secretary.
- The main constraints are structural: Congress, the courts, the budget process, local governments, treaty obligations, and the inherited economy/security environment. The local prior already covers the country-year indicators for rights, corruption, governance, conflict, and welfare, so I did not re-fetch those structured datasets.

**Inherited Conditions / Major 2022 Context**
- Post-pandemic recovery was incomplete.
- Inflation and joblessness were immediate economic priorities.
- The Duterte-era human-rights and press-freedom controversies remained live issues.
- The Philippines also faced South China Sea tensions and repeated disaster exposure, especially typhoons.

**Retained Source Set**
I kept 12 sources total, balancing primary/legal, favorable state-media, independent wire, local-language, and critical families.

Direct constitutional text. Limitation: says what the presidency can do in law, not how Marcos used the office in practice. |

**Compact Event Map**
- **May 25, 2022**: Congress proclaims Marcos president-elect.
- **June 30, 2022**: Marcos is sworn in as the 17th President; EO No. 1 is issued the same day.
- **July 25, 2022**: First SONA sets the agenda around recovery, COVID, education, infrastructure, and sovereignty.
- **August 10, 2022**: Amnesty says the ICC non-rejoin decision will not block investigation.
- **September 24-26, 2022**: Typhoon Noru/Karding hits; Marcos orders work/class suspensions and aid response.
- **October 5, 2022**: PSA reports inflation at 6.9% in September.
- **Late 2022**: HRW’s year-end review says the rights environment remained largely unchanged, with continued killings, red-tagging, and press pressure.

**Search and Rejection Summary**
- I screened roughly 30 documents across BusinessWorld, PNA, Reuters/Euronews syndications, the Singapore MFA, PCO archive pages, White House/State Department materials, AMTI, Brookings, and The Diplomat.
- I rejected later 2023-2026 follow-ups and reposts of the same South China Sea, COC, and alliance themes because they were out of period.
- I collapsed duplicate coverage of the same events where the wording was materially the same, especially the Singapore joint statement, the Biden meeting, and the ASEAN-China COC discussions.
- I dropped domestic-only materials, including Bangsamoro peace-process items and internal governance pieces, because they do not bear directly on this chapter’s international-peace lens.
- I also dropped generic economic or rights articles unless they contained a direct Marcos-attributed international-security choice.
- Some direct palace pages and archive pages were slower or less convenient to fetch; when that happened I used accessible contemporaneous reporting or the corresponding foreign-ministry statement instead.

**Remaining Gaps**
- 2B.4, 2B.5, and 2B.9 remain thin because the Philippines did not conduct an external war in 2022, so there is no real civilian-harm or proxy record to attribute to Marcos in this period.
- 2B.8 is only indirectly covered through alliance-building and maritime posture; I did not find a clean 2022 budget or mobilization record attributable solely to Marcos that would show military spending used for coercive projection.
- 2B.7 is better supported for process than outcome: there were multiple peace/COC statements and meetings, but no binding settlement in 2022.
- More search would help only if you want deeper archival detail on back-channel China diplomacy, defense coordination, or internal cabinet deliberations; it is unlikely to change the basic exposure picture, which is diplomacy-heavy and war-light.
